stem: A high-volume, latency-sensitive routing step classifies incoming messages into six categories. Which tier fits best?

options.text: The most capable available model, for accuracy
The fastest, lowest-cost tier, validated with evals
The mid-tier model with maximum effort
Whichever tier the rest of the application already uses

explanation: Narrow, high-volume, latency-sensitive classification is what the fast, low-cost tier is for, provided evals confirm the quality bar. Defaulting to the most capable model for every task is the classic overprovisioning mistake.
author: legacy

stem: After migrating to a newer model, requests that previously worked return 400 errors on the thinking parameter. What is the likely cause?

options.text: The API key lacks permission for the new model
The newer model runs adaptive thinking and rejects manual thinking budgets
The context window shrank below the request size
Thinking is only available on the Batch API

explanation: Breaking behavior changes across releases are explicitly in scope. Newer models use adaptive thinking with effort as the control and reject manual budget_tokens, which is why migration means reading the guide and re-running evals rather than swapping a model string.
author: legacy

stem: A team migrating to Opus 5 finds their requests now return 400 when they set temperature to 0 for deterministic extraction. What should they do?

options.text: Set temperature to 1 explicitly and accept the variability
Remove the sampling parameter and control output using effort plus a structured output schema
Downgrade to a model that still accepts temperature
Wrap the call in a retry loop until it succeeds

explanation: Non-default sampling parameters return 400 on the newest models; effort has replaced them as the control surface. For deterministic extraction specifically, a structured output schema constrains the shape far more reliably than temperature ever did.
author: legacy

stem: A compliance workflow synthesizes conflicting clauses across long contracts using Claude Sonnet 5 at effort high, and the evals gating this workflow were all tuned against that configuration. Latency is now a concern, so an engineer proposes switching the workflow to Claude Haiku 4.5 at effort low to speed things up while keeping quality about the same. What is wrong with this proposal?

options.text: Nothing is wrong — Haiku 4.5 at effort low will reliably match Sonnet 5's quality on this task
Claude Haiku 4.5 has no effort parameter, and swapping tiers invalidates the evals that were tuned on Sonnet 5's behavior
Effort low always increases latency compared to effort high, so the proposal will make the workflow slower
Claude Sonnet 5 does not support adaptive thinking, so the current baseline is already misconfigured

explanation: Haiku 4.5 is differently shaped, not just cheaper: it runs extended thinking only and has no effort parameter at all, so 'effort low' on Haiku isn't a valid configuration to begin with. Even setting that aside, a tier swap invalidates every eval run against the old model, which is exactly what the workflow's evals were tuned on — the correct move is to step effort down on Sonnet 5 first, not swap tiers. Option A ignores both problems. Option C inverts the actual relationship between effort and latency (lower effort reduces reasoning depth and typically latency, it doesn't guarantee the opposite outcome described). Option D is a false factual claim — Sonnet 5 does support adaptive thinking.
author: v1-new
